Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
718 PM EDT Sat Aug 22 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 254 PM EDT Saturday...

No significant changes have been made to the forecast. The SPC 
Severe Weather Outlook for tomorrow shows the region in a Marginal 
Risk (Level 1 of 5) with the potential for isolated strong to severe 
thunderstorms.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 254 PM EDT Saturday...

1. After a dry and seasonable afternoon, precipitation chances 
will increase across the region tonight through the start of the 
week. 

2. Following a dry midweek period, the next chance for 
scattered showers and thunderstorms arrives in the late Thursday to 
Friday timeframe.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 254 PM EDT Saturday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: After a stretch of dry and seasonable weather the last 
few days, shower chances will return later tonight through the 
weekend. The main feature driving precipitation chances is a large 
upper level trough approaching from the Great Lakes. A frontal 
boundary associated with the parent low will move through tomorrow 
afternoon, driving the chances for scattered showers and 
thunderstorms through the afternoon. Model guidance shows modest 
instability tomorrow afternoon, with CAPE values of 500 J/kg or so 
depending on the location, although there is some uncertainty as to 
how much cloud cover lingers through the morning and inhibits 
afternoon heating. While it's not the most impressive environment, 
there should be enough instability, shear, and forcing to drive 
thunderstorm development tomorrow afternoon. SPC currently shows 
nearly all of the forecast area in a Marginal Risk for severe 
weather tomorrow, meaning that a few isolated strong to severe 
thunderstorms are possible, with possible hail and strong winds as 
the primary threats. The most likely time frame for thunderstorms 
will be from noon through about 7PM, so be sure to monitor the 
forecast if you have any outdoor plans. Storms looks to be 
progressive, limiting any hydro concerns at this time, especially 
given the dry weather the last few days. Current rainfall forecasts 
generally show about 0.25 to 0.50 inches of rain across the area, 
with lower amounts near the International Border and higher amounts 
possible within any thunderstorms. 

For the start of the week, the region will remain in broad cyclonic 
flow, will will allow for linger showers on Monday and Tuesday, 
especially across the higher terrain. This cyclonic flow will also 
lead to some lake effect showers off Lake Ontario, with increased 
shower chances expected across northern New York during this time 
period. Temperatures will be on the cool side, with highs only 
climbing into the 70s, with some locations in the Adirondacks 
struggling to climb out of the upper 60s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Long wave troughing appears to remain over the eastern 
US later next week, with the base of the trough to our west. As 
such, the pattern will be somewhat unsettled with chances for 
showers returning late in the week. The low pressure track is 
strongly favored to be well to our north into central or northern 
Quebec, so widespread heavy rain or strong wind is not on the table, 
and deep layer shear appears limited for severe storms at this time. 
Of the latest ensemble scenarios, ones with a bit more amplified 
trough than the mean upper level heights show 0-500 millibar shear 
probabilities exceeding 30 knots at a greater than 30% chance 
(rather than close to 0%). 

Probable hazards for this system would be fairly widespread, general 
thunderstorm potential associated with the system's cold front, 
which may be thermodynamically strong. Machine learning and other 
ensemble guidance does suggest seasonably high instability for late 
August could be present, with a slight preference for stronger 
variety thunderstorms as you go southward (roughly 5% chance of 
severe weather per GEFS). With a faster timing of an incoming cold 
front, this threat may be limited to Thursday, and a slower timing 
would suggest Friday would be a day to watch for thunderstorms, 
especially in Vermont. The latest guidance has trended perhaps a 
little more towards the later timing, consistent with an occluding 
low pressure system and associated slowing eastward progress of a 
cold front. For now, a slight chance of thunderstorms Thursday 
evening, and slight chance to chance Friday afternoon in most of the 
region, seems reasonable at this point. Given the amount of outdoor 
activities anticipated on Friday and large scale setup for 
thunderstorm potential, this will be a period to keep a close eye.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z SUNDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Through 00Z Monday...Conditions are mainly VFR, although some
lower MVFR ceilings are encroaching on KRUT. As southeast low-
level winds increase, that layer may scatter out at times.
At least some mixing overnight will likely maintain 3-8 knot
across the region, and it will help slowly bring in moisture
that should result in lowering ceilings at KMPV and KEFK. It may
also bring brief LLWS at KMSS, through 12z, but it's not noted
at this time. After sunrise, rising condensation levels should 
bring those areas back to VFR ahead of the main region of lower 
ceilings associated with an occluding frontal boundary. This 
boundary will bring showers and a few embedded thunderstorms as
well. The exact timing of precipitation is challenging with
little consensus, and there could be waves of rain involved. 
Highest confidence is in southeast to south winds increasing to 
8 to 11 knots sustained with a few gusts 15 to 20 knots. 
Thinking showers and storms will be most likely 15z-22z, but 
used PROB30s for most due to uncertainty with respect to timing.
Storms could produce lightning, strong gusts, and heavy rain 
reducing ceilings and visibility. Behind the boundary, ceilings 
are likely to drop towards 1500-4000 ft agl, and winds will 
begin to shift south to southwesterly beyond 00z.

Outlook...
